# AI Usage

The assignment asks candidates to state clearly which code was written by hand
and which was produced with AI tools. This is that statement, written plainly.

## Summary

**Most of the code in this repository was generated by Claude (Anthropic) in a
single working session, with me directing the work, running everything, and
making the scope and debugging decisions.** I did not type the majority of the
implementation myself. Stating otherwise would be inaccurate and easy to
disprove.

## What was AI-generated

- SQL schema in `db/init.sql`
- Vietful emulator (`apps/vietful-emulator/index.js`)
- Collector, worker, webhook controller, Excel controller, hash utility, and
  database service in `apps/cdms/src/`
- `docker-compose.yml` and both Dockerfiles
- The three failure-injection scripts in `scripts/`
- First drafts of `README.md` and `docs/DESIGN.md`

## What I contributed

- Choice of stack. I work in NestJS, Next.js and Postgres, so I chose NestJS
  over the Python implied by the brief's reference to the `faker` library, and
  accepted the `@faker-js/faker` substitution that follows from it.
- Scope decisions under time pressure. I had roughly two working days, not the
  full window, so I sequenced the work: core pipeline first, then webhook, then
  failure testing, then Excel. I chose to write the design document early rather
  than leave it to the end.
- Running and debugging every step. Several problems only appeared at runtime
  and I worked through each one: a local Postgres instance shadowing the
  container on port 5432, a stray `src/` directory created in the wrong working
  directory, TypeScript type errors around multer, and an editor/terminal
  conflict that corrupted a file mid-edit.
- Deciding when a test result was wrong rather than the system. When the crash
  test reported zero pending events, and when the mutation test produced no
  changes, the instinct to accept the green output was wrong both times — the
  tests were flawed, and finding that out drove two of the entries in the
  lessons-learned section.

## Honest assessment of my understanding

I understand the core design and can explain it without notes: why only changes
are stored, why a content hash is used instead of field-by-field comparison, why
the transaction boundary is where exactly-once actually happens, and why there
are two layers of deduplication rather than one.

I am less confident on the details I have not worked with before this weekend —
`FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` semantics under real concurrency, and the internals of
`pg` connection pooling beyond the specific failure I hit and fixed. I would
want to read more before claiming fluency there.

## Why I am stating this plainly

The brief asks for it, and a prototype built this way is only useful if the
reader knows how it was built. I would rather be assessed on what I actually
understand and decided than on an inflated account of authorship.
